topic: What an error budget is in an SLO agreement
stem: In an SLO agreement covering a Claude-based service, what is an error budget?

options.text: A financial provision set aside to pay service credits to users when the service misbehaves.
The maximum number of retries a client may issue with backoff before a request is abandoned.
The quantity of failure the target permits over the window, consumed as failures occur and used to govern releases.
The proportion of the offline evaluation set the team has agreed to treat as permanently unfixable failures.

explanation.correct: Setting a target below 100% is the same as declaring how much failure is acceptable, and the budget makes that quantity explicit and spendable. Its real function is behavioural: while budget remains, the team may take deployment risk; when it is exhausted, the policy attached to it forces a change — freeze releases, divert effort to reliability, or renegotiate the target. Without that attached policy the budget is just arithmetic. It is what turns an aspiration into something that changes engineering decisions week to week.

distractors.A: Service credits are a commercial remedy attached to an SLA breach. They compensate after the fact and have no influence on how the team allocates work, which is the point of an error budget.
distractors.B: Retry limits are a client-side resilience setting. They affect how a single request behaves under failure, not how much aggregate failure the service is permitted across a measurement window.
distractors.D: An eval set is an offline measurement instrument, not the production population an SLO is defined over. Writing off part of it would mean giving up on a class of behaviour, which is a very different decision.

explanation.concept: An error budget is the permitted failure quantity implied by an SLO target, tracked as a consumable over a defined window, and paired with a policy that changes team behaviour when it runs out. A budget with no attached policy provides no control.
explanation.tip: If an option describes money, retries or offline test data, it is not an error budget. The budget is always about production failure volume over a window, and always has a consequence attached.

topic: Compressing an architecture decision for an executive committee
stem: A water utility's architecture board has approved an eight-page ADR choosing an orchestrator–workers design over a single agent for permit-application processing, on the grounds of trajectory auditability, failure containment between steps, and a stated increase in cost per application. The CIO has three minutes at the executive committee. What framing should the architect supply?

options.text: The pattern names and the measured token overhead per application of each design, since the committee funds the technology and should understand what it is buying.
The cost-per-application increase on its own, quoted as an annual figure, since cost is the only dimension an executive committee can meaningfully act on.
A note that the orchestrator–workers choice is technical and internal to the architecture board, so no executive committee time is required.
Regulator-reconstructable permit decisions and failures contained to one step, at the stated increase per application, with the full ADR linked.

explanation.correct: Executive framing is not simplification, it is re-expression in the audience's decision terms. The committee cannot evaluate orchestrator–workers, but it can absolutely evaluate whether regulator-grade traceability and contained failure are worth a named increase per application — that is a value judgement they are accountable for. Keeping the ADR as the linked substrate means nothing is hidden, and the three minutes are spent on the trade-off rather than on vocabulary. Both sides of the trade must be present; a briefing carrying only benefits is not a decision briefing.

distractors.A: Pattern names and token overheads are the right content for the architecture board and the wrong content here. The committee will either nod without understanding or spend the three minutes learning terminology instead of weighing the trade-off.
distractors.B: Presenting the cost with no account of what it buys invites the committee to reject it on price. Cost alone is not a trade-off, and the audit and containment properties are exactly the sort of thing an executive body exists to weigh.
distractors.C: A recurring per-application cost increase and a commitment about regulator traceability are both squarely executive matters. Withholding them because the mechanism is technical is how architecture decisions become surprises later.

explanation.concept: Executive framing translates a technical decision into the organisation's own units of value and cost, states both sides, and links to the full reasoning rather than reproducing it. Never strip the trade-off down to one side, and never treat a decision with recurring cost or external commitments as internal.
explanation.tip: The tell for a correct executive-framing option is that it contains a benefit expressed in business terms and a cost, both. Options carrying only one half are wrong regardless of how well written they are.

topic: Answering a second-vendor mandate with portability rather than dual-running
stem: An insurer's procurement director mandates a second model vendor 'so we are not dependent on one supplier' for a Claude-based claims-summary service handling 9,000 claims a day. The team's prompt library, guardrails, output validators and 1,400-case eval suite are all tuned to the incumbent. What should the architect propose?

options.text: Run both vendors active-active with claims traffic split between them, so failover is continuously proven in production rather than rehearsed.
Sign a standby contract with the second vendor to satisfy the mandate, but route no live claims traffic to it until a switch is actually needed.
Address concentration risk through portability: an abstraction boundary, versioned prompt and eval assets, and a rehearsed migration with the switch time recorded.
Decline the mandate on the grounds that prompts, guardrails and output validators tuned to one model do not transfer, making a second vendor technically unachievable.

explanation.correct: The director's concern is legitimate — being unable to leave a supplier is a real risk — but the demand names a solution rather than the requirement. The requirement is demonstrable exit capability, and that is satisfied by a rehearsed migration, not by continuous dual-running. The rehearsal produces exactly the evidence procurement needs: how long a switch takes and what quality it costs, both measured rather than asserted. It also keeps the insurer running one tuned stack, one safety posture and one eval baseline, which is where the ongoing cost of the alternative actually sits.

distractors.A: Active-active doubles the surface that must be tuned, guardrailed, evaluated and incident-managed forever, and splitting 9,000 daily claims across two models means claims handlers see two quality distributions with no single baseline to hold anyone to.
distractors.B: A contract with no tested path is procurement theatre. The first attempt to use it happens under incident conditions with untested prompts, which is precisely the situation the mandate was meant to prevent.
distractors.D: Prompts and guardrails do need re-tuning across providers, and that cost is real and worth quantifying — but presenting it as an impossibility is both untrue and the answer most likely to be read as vendor lock-in the architect is unwilling to address.

explanation.concept: Separate concentration risk from active redundancy. Portability — an abstraction boundary, provider-independent prompt and eval assets, and a rehearsed migration with measured switch time and quality delta — usually satisfies the governance requirement at a fraction of the cost of running two tuned stacks.
explanation.tip: When a stakeholder states a solution rather than a requirement, name the underlying requirement first. 'Second vendor' is a solution; 'demonstrable ability to exit within a stated time' is the requirement, and it has cheaper answers.

topic: Elements of a usable residual risk statement after guardrails
stem: A local authority children's-services department has deployed input and output guardrails around a Claude-based case-note summarisation tool. The information governance board asks the architect for a written residual risk statement. Which TWO elements make the statement usable by the board rather than merely reassuring? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: An assurance from the architect that the guardrails reduce the risk to a level the department can accept.
The measured rate at which guardrails failed to block a known adversarial test set, with its date and size.
A statement that residual risk falls to zero once both the input and output guardrail layers are enabled.
The detection and response path when a failure gets through: who is alerted, by what signal, and the time to containment.
The model provider's published safety documentation and system card for the underlying model.

explanation.correct: A residual risk statement earns its name by describing what remains after the controls, in terms the board can act on. The measured leak rate against a known adversarial set, with its date and size, tells the board how much confidence the number deserves and when it goes stale. The detection and response path tells them what happens on the day a failure occurs, which is the only part of the statement that operates once prevention has already failed. Together they let the board accept a risk knowingly rather than accept a reassurance.

distractors.A: Acceptability is the board's determination, not the architect's. Supplying the conclusion rather than the evidence removes the board's ability to disagree and leaves nothing on the record to re-examine when the system changes.
distractors.C: This is untrue for any guardrail arrangement and would collapse the first time a case reaches the press. Claiming zero residual risk also removes the justification for the detection and response investment the department needs.
distractors.E: Provider documentation describes the model in general, not this department's deployment, prompts, data or user population. It cannot quantify what remains after controls that the provider knows nothing about.

explanation.concept: Residual risk is what is left after controls, and it is never zero. A usable statement quantifies the leak with a dated, sized test, and describes detection and response for the failures that get through. Reassurance and third-party documentation are not substitutes for either.
explanation.tip: Filter residual risk options by asking whether the board could act differently on the strength of them. A conclusion, a zero claim, and a vendor PDF change no decision; a measured rate and a response path both do.

topic: Resetting expectations after a hand-picked demo
stem: A university's student-services team demonstrated a Claude-based enquiry assistant using twelve hand-picked questions. Every answer was excellent and the pro-vice-chancellor now expects that quality across all enquiries. What correction matters most before the pilot is scoped?

options.text: Extend the demonstration to fifty hand-picked questions drawn from the same enquiry categories, so confidence rests on a broader base before the pilot is scoped.
Say the twelve questions were hand-picked, and re-set expectations against a random sample of real enquiry traffic, malformed and out-of-scope included.
Explain that demonstration quality is unrepresentative because demos run without production latency, rate limiting and concurrent load.
Add an interface disclaimer telling students that answers may be incorrect and should be checked with a member of student-services staff.

explanation.correct: The gap between demo and production here is entirely a sampling artefact: twelve questions someone chose are not a sample of what students ask, and real enquiry traffic contains ambiguous, multi-part, out-of-scope and badly typed questions that a curated set omits. Correcting the expectation requires replacing the selected set with a random draw from actual traffic and quoting the result from that. Doing this before scoping is what stops the pilot being judged against a number that was never achievable.

distractors.A: Fifty selected questions carry the same selection bias as twelve, just with more apparent authority. Sample size does not cure a sampling method that filters out exactly the cases the system will struggle with.
distractors.C: Latency and rate limiting are genuine demo-to-production differences, but they affect responsiveness, not answer quality. Offering this as the explanation misdiagnoses the gap and will be disproved as soon as quality drops in a fast environment.
distractors.D: A disclaimer transfers the problem to students and does nothing about the sponsor's expectation, which is the thing that will determine whether the pilot is judged a success or a failure.

explanation.concept: Expectation set by a curated demo is expectation set on a biased sample. Reset it by measuring on a random draw from real traffic, including the malformed and out-of-scope inputs, and quote that figure as the one the project will be held to.
explanation.tip: Whenever a stem says the demo inputs were chosen by a human, the defect is selection bias. Options that enlarge the curated set or explain the gap by infrastructure differences are both missing it.

topic: Availability target bounded by a serial upstream dependency
stem: A port operator is asked by a shipping-line customer to sign a 99.95% monthly availability SLA for a Claude-based container-documentation checker. Each check calls, in series, the operator's gateway, the model provider, and a national customs reference API whose owner publishes 99.5% availability and offers no better tier. What should the architect say?

options.text: Sign the 99.95% target and add aggressive retry with exponential backoff against the customs API, since retries recover the large majority of transient failures.
Sign the 99.95% target but exclude from measurement every minute in which the national customs API is unavailable, so the figure reflects only what the port operator itself controls.
Offer 99.95% on the model call in isolation, which is the component the SLA is really about, and leave the gateway and customs integration out of scope.
A serial chain cannot exceed its weakest link, so 99.5% caps the achievable figure: renegotiate the target, or serve customs data from a cache with a stated staleness bound.

explanation.correct: Availability of components in series multiplies, so a dependency published at 99.5% puts a ceiling below the requested 99.95% before the operator's own gateway or the model provider are even counted. That is arithmetic, not negotiation, and saying so early is the whole job. It also points at the only two real remedies: change the number, or change the architecture so the weak dependency is not on the synchronous path. Caching customs reference data with an explicit staleness bound is a design change the customer must accept knowingly, which is why it belongs in the SLA text.

distractors.A: Retries help with brief transient errors and do nothing about the sustained unavailability that a 99.5% figure implies. They also consume the latency budget, so the service can end up slower and still outside the target.
distractors.B: Carving out a dependency is legitimate when it is genuinely the customer's own choice of integration. Here the customs check is intrinsic to the product being sold, so excluding it produces a number that no longer describes anything the shipping line experiences.
distractors.C: Scoping the SLA to one internal component leaves the customer with a commitment on something they never invoke directly. Component-level targets are useful internally for allocating budget across a chain, not as the external contract.

explanation.concept: For dependencies in series, composite availability is bounded by the product of the parts, so no target can exceed the weakest link. The honest responses are to renegotiate the target or to remove the weak dependency from the synchronous path — and any degraded mode must be defined in the agreement.
explanation.tip: When a stem hands you an availability figure for one upstream and a higher figure being requested for the whole, the arithmetic has already decided the item. Look for the option that says so rather than the one that engineers around it.

stem: How do an SLI, an SLO and an SLA differ?

options.text: An SLI is the internal target, an SLO is the customer-facing promise, and an SLA is the schedule of penalties attached to that promise.
An SLI covers latency, an SLO covers availability, and an SLA covers output quality such as summary faithfulness.
An SLI is the measurement, an SLO the target set on it, and an SLA the external commitment with consequences attached.
An SLI and an SLO are interchangeable terms; an SLA adds a requirement that the metric be monitored continuously in production.

explanation.correct: The three sit in a chain: you cannot set a target without an indicator, and you should not commit contractually to a target you have not been meeting internally. Keeping them distinct matters in negotiation because the SLA is usually set looser than the SLO deliberately — the internal target leaves headroom so that missing it triggers engineering attention long before it triggers a commercial consequence. Collapsing the three into one number removes that buffer and turns every internal wobble into a contractual event.

distractors.A: This inverts the indicator and the objective. An SLI is a measurement, not a target, and describing the SLO as the customer-facing promise removes the distinction between what a team aims for internally and what it will accept penalties for.
distractors.B: None of the three is tied to a particular dimension. Latency, availability and quality can each have an indicator, an objective and, where measurable, a contractual commitment.
distractors.D: SLI and SLO are not synonyms — one is the measurement, the other the target on it. Monitoring is required for all three; it is not what makes something an agreement.

explanation.concept: SLI is the measurement, SLO the internal target on it, SLA the external commitment with consequences. Set the SLO tighter than the SLA so that internal breach is a warning rather than a commercial event.
explanation.tip: Remember the chain measurement to target to commitment. Any option that assigns the three to different subject areas, or makes two of them synonyms, is wrong on definition alone.

topic: Presenting a benefit confounded by concurrent changes
stem: An energy retailer deployed a Claude-based billing-complaint responder in the same month it retrained its complaint-handling team and changed its refund authorisation policy. Average handling time fell 31% over the following quarter, and the programme lead's board paper attributes the whole fall to the assistant. How should the benefit be presented?

options.text: As a 31% combined effect of three simultaneous changes, the assistant's share unattributed, plus a design to isolate it — a held-out team or a staggered regional rollout.
Attributed across the three changes in proportion to their implementation cost, the only objective split available in the programme's own financials.
Attributed in full to the assistant, since it is the only one of the three changes with a direct mechanism for reducing handling time per contact.
Deferred for a full year of data, by which point the effects of the retraining and the policy change will have washed out and the residual improvement can be credited to the assistant.

explanation.correct: Three interventions landed together, so the observed change is a joint effect and no analysis of the aggregate series can separate them. The defensible move is to report exactly that, resisting the pressure to claim the whole number, and to pair the honest statement with a design that will produce attribution — a held-out group, a staggered rollout, or a natural comparison where only one change applied. Overclaiming here is not just imprecise: it sets a benefit baseline the programme will be measured against in the next review.

distractors.B: Cost is not a causal weight. A cheap policy change can move handling time far more than an expensive build, so splitting the benefit by spend produces a number with the appearance of rigour and no evidential basis.
distractors.C: Retraining complaint handlers has an obvious mechanism for reducing time per contact, and so does widening refund authorisation, since it removes escalations. The premise that only the assistant could have caused the fall is simply false.
distractors.D: Training and policy changes produce persistent level shifts, not decaying effects. Waiting a year yields a confounded series that is twelve months longer, while the decision the board needs is now.

explanation.concept: When interventions land together, the measured change is a joint effect and cannot be decomposed after the fact. Report the combined figure honestly and propose a design — held-out group, staggered rollout, or a natural comparison — that will attribute it going forward.
explanation.tip: Count the changes in the stem. If more than one landed in the same window, every option that assigns the whole benefit to one of them is wrong, however plausible its mechanism sounds.

topic: Validating a confidence signal before it gates human review
stem: A mining company's safety function uses Claude to extract hazard observations from free-text shift reports. The HSE director asks for a numeric confidence score on every extraction so supervisors can review anything below 80%. The team can have the model emit a self-assessed confidence field in its structured output within a day, and 900 extractions have already been manually adjudicated. What is the best next step?

options.text: Emit the self-assessed confidence field and set the review threshold at 80% as requested, monitoring supervisor override rates over the first month.
Decline the request and explain that language models cannot produce numeric confidence estimates of any kind for their own extractions.
Test candidate signals against the 900 adjudicated extractions, then set the threshold from the measured separation and supervisor review capacity.
Replace the score with a fixed random 20% review sample of all extractions, which removes the need for any confidence signal.

explanation.correct: The team already holds the instrument that decides this: 900 adjudicated cases against which any candidate signal can be scored for whether low values actually predict errors. A self-reported number that has not been checked against outcomes may separate correct from incorrect extractions well, poorly, or not at all — and supervisors will read it as a probability regardless, routing their scarce attention by a signal that may be noise. Measuring first also lets the threshold be set where the review capacity and the observed error distribution intersect, rather than at a number chosen because it sounds like a lot.

distractors.A: Shipping an unvalidated signal as a safety-review gate is the failure mode this item is about. The 80% figure carries no meaning until something has established what the score predicts, and override monitoring detects the problem only after supervisors have been mis-routed for a month.
distractors.B: Too categorical, and it abandons a legitimate requirement. Useful confidence signals can be constructed — from sampling disagreement, from a verifier, sometimes from self-assessment — the requirement is that they be validated against labelled outcomes before use.
distractors.D: Uniform random sampling is a reasonable fallback if no signal separates errors, and it gives an unbiased quality estimate. But it spends review effort uniformly across cases rather than concentrating it on likely errors, which is exactly what the director asked for and what the adjudicated set could support.

explanation.concept: Any confidence or uncertainty signal used to route human attention must first be validated against labelled outcomes: does a low score actually predict an error? Thresholds are then set from the measured separation and the available review capacity, never from a round number a stakeholder proposed.
explanation.tip: When a stem mentions an existing adjudicated or labelled set, the answer almost always uses it. A stakeholder-proposed threshold with no validation behind it is the trap being set.

topic: Differential costs in a self-host versus hosted API comparison
stem: A public transport authority's CTO proposes replacing the hosted Claude service behind its accessibility-request triage with a self-hosted open-weights model, arguing it 'removes the per-token bill'. Which TWO cost categories must be added on the self-hosted side for the comparison to be honest? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Reserved accelerator capacity sized for peak concurrency, paid through every quiet period whether or not requests arrive.
Maintenance and re-labelling of the triage evaluation set as the authority's accessibility policies change from year to year.
Engineering capacity to run serving infrastructure — upgrades, scaling and on-call — that the hosted service absorbs today.
Human review of triage decisions, which the authority's policy requires before an accessibility request is actioned.
Per-token inference charges levied on every triage request served by the self-hosted model, billed on the same meter as today.

explanation.correct: A comparison is only honest when it counts costs that differ between the options. Self-hosting converts a usage-linked charge into a capacity commitment: accelerators must be provisioned for peak concurrency and are paid through every quiet period, which for a transport authority's daytime-skewed traffic is most of the day. It also transfers an operational burden — serving upgrades, scaling, on-call — onto a team that does not currently carry it, and that burden is people, not infrastructure, so it does not shrink with volume.

distractors.B: Eval maintenance is a real and frequently forgotten cost, but it is incurred identically under both options. Adding it to one side of a comparison inflates that side without changing the true difference between them.
distractors.D: The review requirement comes from the authority's own policy and applies whichever model produces the triage decision. It belongs in the total cost of the capability, not in the delta between two ways of serving it.
distractors.E: Self-hosting is precisely the arrangement in which there is no per-token charge. Including it would double-count the very line the CTO is proposing to remove.

explanation.concept: Build-versus-buy comparisons must be differential. Include only costs that differ between the options, and be explicit that self-hosting swaps variable usage cost for fixed capacity cost plus permanent operational headcount — the latter being the line most often left out.
explanation.tip: On any comparison item, discard options describing costs incurred under both alternatives, however genuine they are. The question is what changes, not what the system costs in total.

topic: Forecasting a prompt-caching saving under spiky traffic
stem: A hotel group's revenue team presents a twelve-month cost forecast for a Claude-based rate-plan explanation service. A large shared policy preamble is sent on every request, and the forecast applies the reduced cached-input cost to 100% of requests. Booking traffic clusters into two daily peaks with long quiet periods overnight and mid-afternoon. What is the correct fix to the forecast?

options.text: Remove the caching assumption entirely and forecast at full input cost throughout the year, as the conservative position.
Enlarge the shared policy preamble so a greater share of every request is cacheable, improving the ratio of cached to uncached input tokens.
Keep the 100% cached assumption and add a contingency percentage to the annual total to cover the uncertainty.
Model an explicit cache-hit rate from the observed arrival pattern and present the saving as a range with the uncached case as the floor.

explanation.correct: A cache entry does not persist indefinitely through an idle period, so the first requests after each quiet stretch pay full input cost and warm the cache for those behind them. With traffic that clusters into two peaks, the hit rate is a function of the arrival pattern and is knowable from existing booking telemetry — which makes it a modellable driver rather than an unknown. Presenting a range anchored on that rate, with the fully uncached case as the floor, gives finance a forecast that survives a quarter where traffic flattens out.

distractors.A: Forecasting at full cost throughout discards a saving the team can actually demonstrate, and consistently over-forecasting has its own cost: budget held against this service cannot be spent elsewhere, and the next forecast is trusted less.
distractors.B: Growing the preamble raises the cost of every cache miss and does nothing about the reporting defect. It is an architectural change proposed as an answer to a forecasting question.
distractors.C: A contingency buffer conceals a driver that is measurable. Finance cannot tell whether the buffer is covering traffic-pattern risk, volume risk or price risk, so it cannot act when the actual driver moves.

explanation.concept: Caching savings depend on hit rate, and hit rate depends on the traffic arrival pattern. Model it explicitly from observed arrivals and present the outcome as a range bounded by the fully uncached case. A saving assumed at 100% is a forecast of the best case, not a forecast.
explanation.tip: Any stem describing spiky or bursty traffic alongside a caching assumption is testing whether you connect the two. The correct option names the hit rate as a driver rather than burying it in a contingency.

topic: Contents of an ADR for a model version pinning decision
stem: A medical device manufacturer's regulatory affairs team requires an ADR covering the decision to pin the Claude model version behind its post-market surveillance complaint classifier. Which THREE items must the ADR state so that a reviewer a year from now can judge whether the decision is still valid? (Choose THREE.)

options.text: Why pinning was chosen over tracking the latest version: any behaviour change triggers re-validation under the quality management system.
The exact token counts of the classifier prompt and its few-shot examples, as measured on the decision date against the pinned model version.
The conditions that require the pin to be revisited, such as a provider deprecation notice or a validated challenger improvement.
The name of the engineer who set the version string in the deployment manifest, the date applied, and the change ticket reference.
The recurring cost the pin imposes: re-validation owed each time it moves, and the risk of one large migration instead of several small ones.

explanation.correct: A reviewer re-examining a pinning decision needs three things: the reason it was made, the conditions that would end it, and what it costs to keep. The reason connects the pin to the quality system rather than to engineering preference. The revisit conditions convert an indefinite decision into one with defined exits, which is what stops a pin quietly becoming permanent. And the recurring cost makes visible the deferred liability — every version skipped makes the eventual migration larger and its re-validation harder to schedule.

distractors.B: Prompt token counts are an implementation measurement that changes with every prompt edit. They tell the reviewer nothing about whether the pinning decision still holds and would be stale within weeks.
distractors.D: Who applied the configuration is provenance, and version control already records it. An ADR captures the decision and its reasoning, not the identity of the person who typed the value.

explanation.concept: A decision that defers change — a version pin, a frozen dependency, a suspended upgrade — must record its rationale, its exit conditions, and the liability it accrues while it holds. Without exit conditions, deferral silently becomes permanence and the migration debt compounds.
explanation.tip: For 'what belongs in an ADR' items, discard anything that version control, a ticket or a deployment manifest already records. The ADR holds reasoning, consequences and revisit triggers — nothing that a tool captures automatically.

topic: Answering an accuracy question before the system exists
stem: A stakeholder asks what accuracy to expect from a Claude-based system the team has not yet built. Which form of answer is most defensible?

options.text: A single figure taken from the closest published benchmark for a task of this kind, cited as the expected accuracy.
A range with its basis stated — comparable systems the team has measured — and the factors that would move it to each end.
A refusal to estimate, on the grounds that nothing can be said until the system exists and has been measured.
The accuracy target the stakeholder has already stated, since that is the requirement the build will be held to anyway.

explanation.correct: A pre-build estimate is a genuine judgement, and it can be made honestly if it carries its own provenance. Naming the comparable systems tells the stakeholder how much the estimate is worth, and naming the factors that would move it toward either end converts the range into something actionable — those factors become the things the team investigates first. This is also what protects the estimate later: when the built system lands near one end, the record shows why, rather than looking like a miss.

distractors.A: A published benchmark measures a different task on a different distribution, and quoting a single figure from it imports precision the team has no basis for. It will be treated as a commitment as soon as it is spoken.
distractors.C: Refusing to estimate is not neutral — the stakeholder still has to plan, and will substitute an assumption of their own that the team will never see. An architect who cannot bound a problem before building it is of limited use at the point where the decision is made.
distractors.D: Echoing the target back converts an aspiration into a prediction. It also removes the one useful signal the stakeholder needed, which is whether the target is plausible at all.

explanation.concept: Estimate under uncertainty with three components: a range rather than a point, the evidence base the range rests on, and the factors that would move the outcome to each end. Refusing to estimate and quoting a borrowed benchmark are both failures — one withholds judgement, the other fakes it.
explanation.tip: In this domain the correct option is usually the one that shows its working. Look for the answer that names its own evidence and the conditions under which it would be wrong.

topic: Service credit clause tied to an unadjudicated quality term
stem: A courier network's largest customer has signed an agreement containing a service credit payable 'whenever a delivery-exception explanation produced by the system is inaccurate'. The clause defines no measurement method, no sample, and no adjudicator. What is the specific defect the architect should raise with legal?

options.text: A financial obligation turns on a per-incident judgement the agreement never defines; a workable clause names the sample, the rubric, the grader and the threshold.
The service credit is too small to alter the supplier's behaviour, so the clause creates an obligation without any real incentive to improve.
Probabilistic systems should not carry output-quality service credits at all, because any such commitment will eventually be breached at scale.
The term 'inaccurate' should be replaced with 'hallucinated', which has an established technical definition in the research literature and is measurable.

explanation.correct: The clause is unbounded in exactly the dimension that costs money. With no sample definition, every individual complaint is a potential claim; with no rubric or grader, whether an explanation was inaccurate is settled by assertion; and with no aggregation window, there is no ceiling on how many claims a bad week can produce. The remedy is not to remove the commitment but to give it measurement apparatus — a defined sample drawn from a defined population, a written rubric, a named grader, a window and a threshold that must be crossed before credits become payable.

distractors.B: Credit size is a commercial calibration and can be renegotiated. It is the wrong problem: a clause that cannot be measured is unworkable whether the credit is large or small.
distractors.C: Quality commitments on probabilistic systems are entirely possible when written as sampled, thresholded and adjudicated obligations. Refusing all of them concedes ground unnecessarily and is not an argument legal can use.
distractors.D: 'Hallucinated' has no crisper contractual meaning than 'inaccurate' — practitioners disagree about its boundaries, and it would still require a grader. Swapping the word leaves every structural defect in place.

explanation.concept: A quality commitment becomes enforceable only when the agreement specifies the population sampled, the sample size, the grading rubric, who grades, the aggregation window and the breach threshold. Absent those, the clause is an open-ended liability decided by the loudest complainant.
explanation.tip: Test any quality clause by asking who decides, on what evidence, over what window. Options that renegotiate the price of the clause or swap its adjective are avoiding the structural defect.

topic: Decision item versus information item in a steering paper
stem: In a steering committee paper, what distinguishes a decision item from an information item?

options.text: A decision item includes the supporting analysis in full; an information item is a one-paragraph summary of delivery progress.
A decision item is tabled by the programme sponsor; an information item is tabled by the delivery team lead.
A decision item concerns budget or scope; an information item concerns delivery progress and milestones.
A decision item names the choice, the options and a recommendation; an information item reports status and asks nothing.

explanation.correct: The distinction is functional, not editorial: it is about whether the committee has to do something before the meeting ends. A decision item must arrive with the choice explicitly framed, the realistic options and what each costs, and a recommendation the committee can accept or overturn — without those, the item consumes time and produces nothing. Mislabelling matters in both directions: an information item dressed as a decision wastes the committee, and a decision buried in a status update gets nodded through with no one accountable for having made it.

distractors.A: Length and depth of analysis vary independently of type. A decision item can be half a page if the choice is clear, and a status update can be long if there is a lot to report.
distractors.B: Who tables an item says nothing about what is being asked of the committee. Delivery teams routinely bring the most consequential choices, and sponsors routinely bring pure status. Authorship is a routing convention, not a classification, and using it as one guarantees decisions arrive unframed.
distractors.C: Subject matter does not determine type either. Budget figures are frequently reported for information only, and a progress update becomes a decision item the moment it forces a re-plan. Classifying by topic means the committee discovers what it is being asked only when someone reaches the last slide.

explanation.concept: Classify papers by the action required, not the topic or the author. A decision item states the choice, the options with consequences, and a recommendation; an information item requires no action. Labelling correctly is what makes committee time productive and accountability traceable.
explanation.tip: The functional definition wins on items like this. Options that key on length, author or subject area are all describing correlates rather than the distinction itself.

topic: Replacing a never-invents-facts claim with a mechanism claim
stem: A property portal's commercial director wants the public product page for a Claude-based listing-description generator to state that the system 'never invents facts about a property'. Descriptions are generated from structured listing fields plus the agent's free-text notes, and a post-generation validator checks each factual assertion back against the source fields. What should the architect propose the page say?

options.text: Retain 'never invents facts' and add small-print advising that generated descriptions should be verified by the listing agent before they are published.
Say the system 'uses advanced AI to ensure accuracy', which conveys the benefit to buyers without committing to a specific measurable claim.
Describe the mechanism: facts drawn from named listing fields, unmatched assertions removed not published, with the validator's measured catch rate.
Make no factuality claim on the product page and address the topic in the terms of service instead, where the general disclaimer already sits.

explanation.correct: A property description is a document a buyer may rely on, so an absolute claim on the public page is a misrepresentation exposure that fails the first time a single description slips through. What the portal actually has is stronger than a slogan and fully defensible: a grounding constraint, an automated check, and a removal rather than a guess when the check fails. Publishing the mechanism plus the measured catch rate is verifiable, survives the first failure without being falsified, and differentiates the portal from competitors whose page says nothing but 'accurate'.

distractors.A: The disclaimer contradicts the headline, and a small-print caveat does not cure a categorical representation made prominently on a product page. It also invites the reasonable question of why verification is needed if the system never invents anything.
distractors.B: This is vaguer but still an accuracy claim, and it is unmeasurable, so the portal cannot defend it or improve against it. Replacing a falsifiable overclaim with an unfalsifiable one is a step backwards.
distractors.D: Burying it in terms of service abandons a real and demonstrable strength, and leaves the buyer with no statement at all about how descriptions are produced — which for a document buyers rely on is worse for the portal, not safer.

explanation.concept: Never commit to an absolute outcome for a probabilistic system. Commit instead to the mechanism, the check that enforces it, the behaviour when the check fails, and the measured rate at which it fires. A mechanism claim is verifiable, improvable, and survives an individual failure.
explanation.tip: Any option containing 'never', 'always' or 'guaranteed' about model output is wrong in this domain. The correct answer converts the outcome claim into a process claim with a number attached.

topic: Comparing a measured option against an unbuilt one honestly
stem: A film studio's post-production group must choose between two designs for a Claude-based dialogue-continuity checker. Option 1 has been prototyped and measured on 500 scenes. Option 2 exists only as a design. The proposed slide puts both into one table with accuracy, latency and cost-per-episode columns, all shown as single figures. Which TWO changes make the comparison honest? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Drop Option 2 from the table until it has been prototyped and measured to the same standard as Option 1 was.
Mark each cell with its provenance — measured on 500 scenes, vendor-supplied, or engineering estimate — so rows can be weighted.
Show the unbuilt option's cells as ranges with the assumption driving each, not point values identical in form to measured ones.
Collapse the three columns into a single weighted score so the two options can be ranked without the reader having to interpret them.
Show only the accuracy column, since latency and cost per episode cannot be known for an option that has not been built.

explanation.correct: The dishonesty in the table is entirely visual: a measured figure and a guess rendered in the same font in adjacent cells read as equally solid. Provenance labels break that equivalence directly, and are cheap enough that there is no reason not to. Ranges do the same work in the other dimension, forcing the estimate to display its own width, and attaching the driving assumption tells the reader which estimate would move if that assumption turned out wrong. Neither change removes information; both stop the format asserting confidence the data does not have.

distractors.A: The decision on the table is partly whether to invest in prototyping Option 2, so removing it makes that decision impossible. An unmeasured option can be compared honestly; it just cannot be displayed as though it were measured.
distractors.D: A weighted composite compounds the problem. It hides which inputs were estimated, buries the weighting judgement inside a single number, and produces a ranking that looks more authoritative than any of the figures underneath it.
distractors.E: Latency and cost for an unbuilt design can be estimated with stated assumptions, and both matter to the choice. Deleting two of three decision axes to avoid uncertainty leaves the group choosing on a single dimension.

explanation.concept: When a comparison mixes measured and estimated figures, the format must show the difference: label provenance per cell and present estimates as ranges with their driving assumptions. Uniform point values across sources are the most common way a slide misleads without containing a false statement.
explanation.tip: False-precision items often hinge on presentation rather than on the numbers. Ask whether the format lets a reader tell what was measured; the two changes that restore that distinction are the keys.

topic: Escalating a run-cost overrun whose fix changes user behaviour
stem: Seven weeks into the quarter, a vehicle manufacturer's aftersales platform team finds its Claude-based warranty-claim assessor is running at 2.4 times forecast cost. The cause is dealers pasting whole service-history PDFs into a free-text field, inflating input tokens. At the current rate the quarterly budget is exhausted in about three weeks. Capping input size would make the assessor reject or truncate the pasted histories dealers currently rely on. The budget owner is the aftersales director, who has not yet been told. What is the best next step?

options.text: Apply the input cap and a summarisation pre-step immediately, then report the overrun to the director once the run rate is back within forecast.
Tell the aftersales director now, with the measured run rate, the cause, the exhaustion date, and both options: fund the overrun, or cap what dealers can submit.
Request a budget increase from the aftersales director framed as unanticipated adoption success, and take the technical analysis to the quarterly review.
Impose a hard per-dealer request quota so spend cannot exceed the quarterly budget, and raise the matter at the next quarterly review.

explanation.correct: The decisive fact is that the cheap technical fix is not cost-neutral to the business: capping input changes what dealers can submit and therefore what the assessor can assess. That makes it a service-level decision belonging to the person accountable for the service and its budget, not an optimisation the platform team can apply on its own authority. Going now, with the measured rate, the diagnosed cause, the exhaustion date and both options priced, gives the director three weeks to choose — which is the difference between a decision and a fait accompli.

distractors.A: Applying the cap silently is the version of this that ends badly. Dealers experience a degraded service, complaints reach the director from the field rather than from the team, and the budget conversation now starts from a loss of trust.
distractors.C: Reframing an unintended usage pattern as adoption success is spin, and deferring the analysis leaves the director funding a driver nobody has explained. It also forgoes the cap option entirely, which may well be the right answer once dealers are consulted.
distractors.D: A per-dealer quota bounds spend but silently rations a production service, with the harshest effect on the highest-volume dealers. Like the cap, it is a service-level change made without the accountable owner, and it is applied with less analysis behind it.

explanation.concept: Escalate a cost overrun when it is diagnosed, not when it is fixed — and always when the available mitigation changes what users experience. Bring the measured rate, the cause, the date of exhaustion, and the priced options. Mitigations with business-visible side effects belong to the budget owner.
explanation.tip: The discriminator in overrun items is whether the fix is invisible to users. If the stem spells out what the mitigation would do to them, the answer is escalation with options, not unilateral action.
